analysis.one_liner: Bans forced arbitration clauses in employment, consumer, civil rights, and antitrust contracts.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 24 cosponsors — all Democrats or independents — but never got a hearing or a vote and died in the Senate Judiciary Committee when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have voided contract clauses that force employees, consumers, and civil rights and antitrust plaintiffs into private arbitration before any dispute arises. It put a court, rather than an arbitrator, in charge of deciding whether an arbitration agreement is valid. It carved out collective bargaining agreements between employers and unions.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and employees with disputes over goods, services, credit, jobs, discrimination, or antitrust violations would regain the right to take their cases to court instead of being locked into private arbitration by contract terms they agreed to before any dispute existed [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, employees, and civil rights plaintiffs

how_it_helps.text: No arbitration agreement signed before a dispute arises could be enforced against an employee, consumer, civil rights plaintiff, or antitrust class plaintiff — people would keep their right to sue in court
A court, applying federal law, would decide whether an arbitration agreement is valid, instead of an arbitrator chosen under the contract itself
Even under collective bargaining agreements, union arbitration provisions could not be used to waive a worker's right to go to court to enforce constitutional or statutory rights

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that write forced arbitration clauses into employment and consumer contracts — banks, credit card issuers, employers, and the arbitration industry — would bear the cost of defending disputes in open court, including class actions [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill's own findings concede arbitration can be acceptable when consent is truly voluntary and happens after a dispute arises; critics of restricting arbitration point out that court cases are slower and more expensive, especially for small claims

Businesses argue that class action litigation mainly benefits plaintiffs' lawyers, and that arbitration is faster and cheaper for resolving everyday disputes — the bill would push all covered disputes into court

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have restored a genuine choice for millions of workers and consumers by striking forced arbitration clauses from employment and consumer contracts, at real cost to the banks, employers, and arbitration firms that rely on them. The strongest honest objection is that court litigation is slower and costlier than arbitration for small individual claims, and that the bill eliminated even agreements both parties might voluntarily make before a dispute.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or vote, and died when the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Al Franken introduced the bill on April 29, 2015, with 15 original cosponsors
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee the same day, and no further action followed
It drew 24 cosponsors — 23 Democrats and 1 independent — before Congress ended on January 3, 2017

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks, employers, and the arbitration industry kept the ability to require workers and consumers to resolve disputes in private arbitration rather than court. Consumers and employees who might have regained court access are no better off.

for.name: Sen. Al Franken
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 15 original cosponsors

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing or vote on it

against.name: Arbitration industry and business groups
against.role: Financial services companies, major employers, and arbitration providers
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on mandatory pre-dispute arbitration clauses

sides.party_line_note: All 24 cosponsors were Democrats or independents, including Bernie Sanders; no Republicans signed on, and the Republican-led Judiciary Committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: For-profit arbitration providers' core business — processing millions of forced-arbitration employment and consumer disputes — would have been largely eliminated for these case types. Their gain under the status quo is ordinary people's loss of court access.
Banks and card issuers use arbitration clauses to bar customers from joining class actions over fees and other disputes. The bill would have exposed them to those lawsuits in court.
Employers routinely require workers to sign pre-dispute arbitration agreements covering workplace disputes, including discrimination claims. The bill would have moved those cases back into court.
